overview: Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections, according to Wikipedia's news summary, and the aftermath is shaping the day: Republicans are debating a delay to Senate leadership votes, and a House impeachment vote against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is expected. The Supreme Court let the administration temporarily resume border construction in Texas' Big Bend area, and California voters rejected a one-time tax on billionaires' wealth. Abroad, U.S. envoys renewed Russia-Ukraine peace talks, France blamed Iran for a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration, and six people were killed in a shooting in Kraków, Poland. In markets, a Federal Reserve governor's call for a December rate hike came hours before today's inflation report.

stories.headline: House faces vote on Massie's bid to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
stories.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, moved on Monday to force a House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war. President Trump defended Hegseth, and Hegseth is scheduled to hold a rare Pentagon briefing Tuesday. A vote is expected this week, days after Republicans lost heavily in the midterms.
stories.why_it_matters: It would be a rare attempt to impeach a Cabinet member from the president's own party, and it tests how much of the GOP will break with Trump over the Iran war after the midterm losses. Outlets tie the war to higher energy prices and inflation, which affect household budgets.
stories.background: Pete Hegseth became defense secretary in 2025 and has rebranded the department as the Department of War. The US has been fighting a war with Iran in 2026, and outlets say it raised energy prices and hurt Republicans in last week's midterms. Massie lost a Trump-backed primary earlier this year and first introduced impeachment articles against Hegseth in September. The new articles accuse Hegseth of waging war without congressional approval and of other misconduct. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is backing the effort, according to NewsNation.

facts.text: Massie moved Monday, Nov. 9, to force a House vote on impeaching Hegseth, France 24 reported.
The Hindu reports the resolution contains eight articles of impeachment and is backed by lawmakers including Rep. Ro Khanna.
Reuters reported that a House impeachment vote is expected this week.
Trump called Massie a 'total loser' and said Hegseth should be 'praised, not impeached.'
Massie told CNN he sees a 'high probability' Hegseth will not be in the job by the new year.
NewsNation reports the articles accuse Hegseth of waging war without Congress's approval, and that Jeffries backs the effort.
Hegseth is set to hold his first Pentagon news briefing since May on Tuesday morning, CBS News reported.
Massie first introduced impeachment articles against Hegseth in September, according to CNN reporting syndicated by local stations.

stories.headline: Supreme Court lets Trump administration resume border wall construction in Big Bend
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday lifted a lower-court injunction that had halted border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, which includes parts of Big Bend National Park. The environmental groups' lawsuit continues. The administration said it adjusted its plans to preserve the landscape and public access, per the New York Times.
stories.why_it_matters: Construction can now proceed in a remote national-park area while the legal challenge plays out, affecting landowners, visitors and the border region's environment. It is also another instance of the justices acting on the emergency docket.
stories.background: In early October a federal judge in El Paso, Kathleen Cardone, blocked further construction in Big Bend, finding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in arguing the homeland security secretary's waivers of environmental laws exceeded his authority. The administration asked the Supreme Court on Oct. 21 to pause that order, skipping the appeals court. Preservation and environmental groups opposed, warning construction could begin immediately. The Court's order does not end the underlying lawsuit.

The administration filed an emergency request in October asking to continue construction while the lawsuit proceeds, NPR reported.
The Guardian reports the ruling said a law enacted by Congress reflects a preference for border control over environmental and recreational harm.
The administration said it adjusted construction plans in the park to preserve the landscape and public access, according to the New York Times.

stories.headline: Senate Republicans hold leadership vote as faction pushes to delay it after midterm losses
stories.summary: Senate Republicans are scheduled to hold leadership elections Tuesday for the next Congress, when they will be in the minority. Axios reported seven GOP senators want the vote delayed and that Majority Leader John Thune is still expected to be re-elected. Meanwhile House Republicans are preparing their own leadership elections.
stories.why_it_matters: Who leads each party's caucus shapes what Congress does in the lame-duck session and how Republicans handle being in the minority, including what happens to Trump's remaining priorities.
stories.background: John Thune became Senate majority leader in 2025. Republicans lost control of Congress in last week's midterms, and the new Congress begins in January. A group of conservatives wants more time to discuss the losses and to extract a plan for the lame-duck session. Sen. Ron Johnson circulated a letter seeking a delay, according to the Daily Signal. Thune has said he plans to go ahead.

facts.text: Seven Republican senators were calling for the leadership elections to be delayed, one promising to walk out rather than vote, Axios reported; it said Thune was still expected to be re-elected.
Sen. Rick Scott said he will not back Thune without a specific plan for the lame-duck session, Fox News reported.
The Washington Examiner reports Thune is proceeding with Tuesday's elections despite calls for a post-midterm reckoning.
The Hill reports House Republicans are preparing to elect a new leadership team as they move into the minority.
The Daily Signal reported Sen. Ron Johnson gathered signatures on a letter demanding a delay.

stories.headline: Stephen Miller starts as White House chief of staff; Trump holds surprise briefing
stories.summary: Stephen Miller began work Monday as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles, after Trump announced the change on Nov. 6. Trump then held an unannounced briefing with UFC chief Dana White, who declined an offer of the press secretary job, and defended Hegseth and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
stories.why_it_matters: Miller, the architect of Trump's immigration crackdown, now runs day-to-day White House operations, which may shape how the administration deals with a Democratic-led House on immigration, spending and oversight.
stories.background: Susie Wiles had been chief of staff since Trump's 2025 return to office. Trump announced the swap days after Republicans lost control of Congress. Miller was a deputy chief of staff and is known as the driver of the administration's mass-deportation policy. Reaction was mixed: Vice President Vance congratulated him, while Democrats and some Republicans criticized the choice, per syndicated AP coverage.

stories.headline: Trump says Iran war is militarily 'effectively over' after meeting Qatar's prime minister
stories.summary: After meeting Qatar's prime minister on Monday, Trump said the war with Iran is militarily 'effectively over,' that it should end 'fairly soon,' and that new strikes are not needed. He said the US is keeping its wartime posture in the region to protect Gulf allies and that there is a 'good chance' of a deal.
stories.why_it_matters: A wind-down of the war could ease the energy prices and inflation that outlets link to it, and it bears on US troop deployments and the Hegseth impeachment fight.
stories.background: The US and Israel began striking Iran in late February 2026. Qatar has been a main mediator, and earlier reporting describes a Qatar- and Pakistan-mediated memorandum with a ceasefire and a timetable for a final deal. The war and its effects on energy prices have been blamed by outlets for Republicans' midterm losses. Trump has made differing statements about the ceasefire at various points.

stories.headline: Trump says FBI is reviewing Nvidia CEO Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
stories.summary: Trump said he spoke with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and that the FBI is looking into Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence. stories.why_it_matters: The case touches US chip export controls and national security, and it could affect Nvidia, a company central to AI and to many retirement and investment portfolios.
stories.background: Nvidia makes the leading chips used for artificial intelligence, and US rules limit sales of advanced chips to China. Huang told employees he had an extramarital affair, and Nvidia is investigating reported allegations that the woman may have worked for Beijing's intelligence services. stories.headline: US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks resume in Abu Dhabi
stories.summary: Negotiators from Russia and Ukraine began two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the first such meeting since February. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are taking part, and the White House said the focus would be security guarantees. Russia carried out deadly attacks on Ukraine hours before the session, the Guardian reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Any deal could change whether the war that has run for more than four years continues, and what security arrangements apply across Europe. Coverage in the digest comes from left and center outlets plus Fox News, and all describe the talks as early-stage.
stories.background: Russia invaded Ukraine more than four years ago, and the war has continued since. The United States has acted as mediator under President Trump, using envoys Witkoff and Kushner. The last comparable round of talks was in February. Security guarantees for Ukraine, meaning what protection it would have against another invasion, and disputes over territory are the central issues the outlets list.

Kushner and Witkoff are the US envoys in the talks, with negotiators from Russia and Ukraine.
US officials said they are seeking a "final end" to the war, and the Guardian reported the US proposal includes a "long-term security architecture" between Moscow and Europe.
Fox News reported that the envoys are pushing a NATO-like security guarantee for Ukraine and that territory disputes are on the agenda.

stories.headline: Trump says new strikes on Iran are unlikely; Brent falls below $90
stories.summary: President Trump said on Monday that a resumption of the war with Iran is unlikely, and oil prices fell. Brent crude dropped below $90 a barrel for the first time since August, according to CNBC and the Guardian. Iran still partly blocks traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the Hindu reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil prices feed into fuel and transport costs and into inflation, so a sustained drop would ease pressure on household budgets. The situation remains fragile, with analysts cited by CNBC seeing little chance of a lasting peace deal. Digest coverage is left and center only.
stories.background: The United States and Iran have been in a military conflict, with US strikes on Iran and Iranian pressure on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for Gulf oil. Attacks on Saudi Arabia and incidents involving tankers have raised concern about supplies, the Wall Street Journal reported. Negotiations involving Qatar are under way, per Axios. Oil traded near $113 in late October, according to the New York Times.

Axios reported Trump called a renewed campaign "quite unlikely" and said it "doesn't seem to be necessary."

stories.headline: France blames Iran's Revolutionary Guards for supermarket refrigerator cyberattack
stories.summary: The French government attributed an October cyberattack that disrupted refrigeration at roughly 700 supermarkets to a cyber unit of Iran's Revolutionary Guards. Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said he summoned Iran's ambassador and that Paris will seek European action. Iran had not immediately responded, the New York Times reported.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how hacks of everyday systems such as store refrigeration can spoil food and cause fires, and it could lead to new sanctions on Iran. The attribution comes from the French government, and the digest shows no independent confirmation yet.
stories.background: In mid-October, a cyberattack caused refrigerator temperatures to climb at hundreds of French stores, spoiling food. Retailers confirmed the incident and the government opened an investigation. France is now publicly attributing it to the cyber arm of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The accusation comes while Iran is also in conflict with the United States.

facts.text: France's government said an Iranian military hacking unit disrupted refrigeration at roughly 700 grocery and retail locations last month, causing food losses and at least 15 fires, per Axios.
Barrot said he summoned the Iranian ambassador.

CNBC reported France described an "unprecedented campaign" causing millions of euros in damage, and said France is weighing sanctions.

stories.headline: Krakow gunman who killed six in city square has died in hospital
stories.summary: The 24-year-old man who opened fire in a Krakow square, killing six people and wounding at least 15, died in hospital on Monday, police said. Polish authorities opened a terrorism investigation and have described the suspect as holding far-right views. The New York Times reported additional deaths in another town, bringing the total to at least nine.
stories.why_it_matters: Mass shootings are rare in Poland, which has strict gun laws, and the attack is prompting questions about extremism and how a licensed sport shooter could carry it out. The motive is still unclear.
stories.background: The attack happened on Nov. 7 in Krakow's main square. Police shot and wounded the suspect, a Polish citizen with no criminal record who held a sport-shooting licence, per web reports. Prosecutors say the same person is responsible for three further deaths at a home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski. A minister described his views as "ultranationalistic."

stories.headline: China's trade surplus tops $1 trillion for a second straight year
stories.summary: China said its trade surplus passed $1 trillion for the second year running, with October exports up 35%. Outlets attribute much of the surge to global demand for AI-related hardware such as chips and servers. The figure is likely to add to complaints from trading partners.
stories.why_it_matters: A large surplus can mean cheaper imported goods for shoppers but pressure on factories and jobs abroad, and it raises the chance of tariffs and trade disputes. Digest coverage here is left and center; no right-leaning outlets carried it.
stories.background: China sells far more goods abroad than it buys, producing a large surplus. Weak domestic spending and a property slump have made its economy lean on overseas demand, per the Japan Times. Trading partners have complained about the volume of cheap Chinese goods. This year the AI boom added demand for Chinese-made chips, servers and networking equipment.

facts.text: China said its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a second straight year, with October exports up 35%.

stories.headline: Fed's Waller backs a December rate hike and leaves room for a half-point move
stories.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday he supports raising interest rates in December and could back a half-point increase if inflation keeps accelerating. Bloomberg reported the remarks came just hours before the October consumer price report. US stocks had lost momentum after a rebound the day before.
stories.why_it_matters: A rate hike would raise borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans and credit cards, and the inflation data due now will help decide how large it is.
stories.background: The Fed sets short-term interest rates to balance inflation against jobs. Waller is one of the seven members of its Board of Governors, who vote on rate decisions along with regional bank presidents. Reporting this week describes a policy debate about raising rather than cutting rates, with energy prices cited as a driver of inflation. Other central banks are weighing the same question: the Bank of England's Lombardelli did not rule out a December hike, and the ECB's Martins Kazaks said tightening may be needed if high energy prices persist. The October consumer price index is the next major data point before the Fed's December meeting.

facts.text: Waller said he supports a rate increase in December, and said he would support a half-point increase if inflation comes in substantially higher than he expects, to protect the Fed's credibility, according to Bloomberg.
CNBC quoted Waller as saying he is "leaning toward" a December increase, and that a half-point move would depend on inflation data.
Reuters reported Waller plans to support at least a quarter-point hike in December.
MarketWatch said the size of any hike depends on how hot the October consumer price data comes in.
Bloomberg reported a stock market rebound stalled after Waller's remarks, and that gold extended a decline.
Reuters reported the dollar steadied after Waller's comments, with inflation data next.
Bank of England deputy governor Lombardelli told the Guardian she does not rule out a December rate hike, per Reuters.

framing.note: Frames it as a market story: a stock rebound that ran out of steam.
Frames it through gold, a decline extended by the hike signal.

concept.explanation: Brent is the global benchmark price for oil, based on crude pumped from the North Sea and used to price roughly two-thirds of the world's traded oil; U.S. oil is tracked separately as WTI. It moves with supply decisions by producers, stockpile levels and geopolitical risk, such as tension with Iran, which sits beside key shipping routes. It reaches your wallet through gasoline, diesel and airfares first, and then through the cost of shipping goods, which is why central banks watch oil when judging inflation.

quotes.name: S&P 500
quotes.blurb: 500 of the largest US companies. The standard scoreboard for the US stock market.

quotes.name: Nasdaq Composite
quotes.blurb: Heavy on tech companies, so it swings harder than the S&P 500 on tech news.

quotes.name: Dow Jones Industrial Average
quotes.blurb: 30 big, established US companies. The oldest and most quoted index, but narrow.

quotes.name: Fed funds rate
quotes.blurb: The overnight rate the Federal Reserve targets. Every other US interest rate keys off it.

quotes.name: 2-year Treasury yield
quotes.blurb: What the US government pays to borrow for 2 years. Moves with expectations for Fed rate changes.

quotes.name: 10-year Treasury yield
quotes.blurb: The government's 10-year borrowing cost. Mortgage rates and company borrowing costs follow it.

quotes.name: 30-year mortgage rate
quotes.blurb: Freddie Mac's weekly average for a 30-year fixed mortgage.

quotes.name: Inflation (CPI, year over year)
quotes.blurb: How much consumer prices rose over the past year. The Fed aims for about 2%.

quotes.name: Unemployment rate
quotes.blurb: Share of people looking for work who can't find it. From the monthly jobs report.

quotes.name: Crude oil (WTI)
quotes.blurb: US oil price per barrel. Feeds into gas prices and inflation.

quotes.name: Crude oil (Brent)
quotes.blurb: The global oil benchmark. Jumps on Middle East and Russia supply news.

quotes.name: Natural gas (Henry Hub)
quotes.blurb: US natural gas price at the Henry Hub in Louisiana, per million BTU. Drives heating and electricity bills.

quotes.name: US dollar index (broad)
quotes.blurb: The Fed's index of the dollar against the currencies of US trading partners. Up means a stronger dollar.

quotes.name: Euro (USD per EUR)
quotes.blurb: Dollars per euro. Up means the euro strengthened against the dollar.

quotes.name: Japanese yen (JPY per USD)
quotes.blurb: Yen per dollar. Up means a weaker yen.

quotes.name: Chinese yuan (CNY per USD)
quotes.blurb: Yuan per dollar. Beijing manages it closely, so moves are a policy signal.

quotes.name: Bitcoin
quotes.blurb: The largest cryptocurrency. Trades around the clock and swings far more than stocks.
